planting.note: Plant grafted or rooted stock in spring in gritty, well-drained soil; this extremely slow-growing dwarf selection is prized far more for container and bonsai culture than as an in-ground landscape tree.

directions: This dwarf witch's-broom sport of trident maple produces tightly congested, narrow leaves whose elongated center lobe and reduced side lobes give the foliage a slender, blade-like silhouette quite unlike typical trident maple leaves. Growth is markedly slow and twiggy compared with the species, and plants stay compact for many years, which along with fine, dense ramification makes it a favorite for shohin and mame-sized bonsai. Fall color still runs through yellow, orange, and maroon, often on the same tree at once. It is difficult to propagate true-to-type, which keeps it uncommon in the nursery trade and best sourced from specialist maple growers.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; the curled foliage is the main ornamental draw, so give it a site where the leaf texture can be appreciated up close.

directions: Naruto is named for the whirlpools off the Japanese coast, a nod to its distinctive leaves, whose three lobes curl and roll inward along the margins instead of lying flat, giving the crown an almost ruffled, birds-in-flight texture that sets it apart from any other trident maple selection. It grows into a small to medium tree considerably faster and larger than dwarf yatsubusa-type cultivars, reaching around 15 feet over two decades, and shares the species' tolerance of heat, drought, and urban soils once established. Fall color develops in strong orange-red tones. Its unusual foliage and manageable scale make it popular both as a specimen tree and as material for larger bonsai and penjing work.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant nursery stock in spring in fast-draining succulent mix in bright light; this form is noticeably more cold-sensitive and slower-growing than plain-green spekboom.

directions: This sport of elephant bush carries small, glossy rounded leaves edged and marbled in cream to white, often flushing pink under bright light or cool temperatures, on the same reddish woody stems typical of the species. Growth is slower and the plant stays more compact than the plain green form, so it is widely grown as a houseplant, patio succulent, or bonsai subject where its foliage color can be shown off. Give it bright, filtered to morning sun rather than harsh full afternoon exposure, since intense direct sun can scorch the paler variegated tissue while too little light causes reversion to plain green growth. It has the same low water needs as the species but is markedly less cold-hardy, so plan to bring it indoors well before frost.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in lean, fast-draining soil; use in hanging baskets, raised beds, or as a cascading accent over walls and container edges rather than as an upright shrub.

directions: Also sold as 'Minima', this selection of elephant bush grows laterally along arching stems rather than upright, forming a low mat or cascade instead of the shrubby, tree-like habit of the species. Small glossy round leaves cover trailing branches that root readily wherever they touch soil, making it useful as a groundcover in frost-free gardens or as a spiller in mixed succulent containers and hanging pots. Occasional small pink to pale purple flowers appear on established plants. It shares the species' drought tolerance and easy propagation from stem or leaf cuttings but needs protection from any freezing temperatures.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in light shade to morning sun in spring or fall; some afternoon shade helps protect the variegated leaf margins from scorching in hot climates.

directions: Goshiki, meaning "five colors" in Japanese, is a slow-growing variegated sport of Japanese zelkova whose leaves emerge in soft shades of cream, pink, and green before settling into a bolder pattern of dark green centers edged and flecked with white through summer, then shifting to yellow, orange, and red in fall. It matures into the same graceful, vase-shaped, multi-trunked silhouette as the species but stays noticeably smaller and grows more slowly, making it better suited to smaller gardens or as a specimen accent than a full-scale shade tree. Like other zelkova selections it belongs to the elm family and resists Dutch elm disease. Because variegation can be lost on vigorous watersprouts, prune out any shoots that revert to solid green.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil in spring or fall; allow ample room, since this species eventually develops an unusually dense, broadly upright crown of many erect branches from a short trunk.

directions: Native to the Hyrcanian and Colchic forests of the Caucasus and northern Iran, this relative of the more familiar Japanese zelkova is a large, long-lived tree that develops a short, stout trunk from which dozens of nearly vertical branches arise, producing a dense, broom-like or globe-shaped crown unlike the open vase form of Zelkova serrata. Its neatly toothed, oval leaves are rich green through the growing season and turn orange-brown in autumn. It is considerably less common in cultivation than Japanese zelkova and grows more slowly, but old specimens in European parks and Caucasian village courtyards are prized as long-lived shade trees. In the wild it is classified as vulnerable, so cultivated and arboretum-grown trees also serve a conservation role.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant in full sun in gritty, well-drained mountain-type soil in spring; this is a slow-growing collector's tree suited to botanic gardens, arboreta, and dedicated plant collections rather than mainstream landscape use.

directions: Endemic to the mountains of Crete, this is one of the smallest and rarest members of the zelkova genus, forming a dense, low-branched, shrubby crown that can extend nearly to the ground rather than the tall, clean-trunked shade tree habit of its Asian relatives. Small, finely serrated leaves cover twiggy branches, and the species spreads locally by root suckers, since seed regeneration in the wild is scarce. Classified as near threatened due to grazing pressure, drought, and traditional harvesting of branches for walking sticks, it is grown outside its native range mainly by botanic gardens and specialist collectors as a conservation and curiosity planting. It is slow-growing and long-lived, tolerating thin mountain soils and periods of summer drought once established.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; give it generous room to spread, since it covers ground considerably faster and wider than 'Nana'.

directions: Collected on Japan's Bonin Islands and sometimes confused with the far more common 'Nana', this selection of Japanese garden juniper is a noticeably stronger, faster-growing plant with coarser blue-green needle foliage on stiffly spreading branches. It forms a broad, low mat useful for covering large areas quickly, stabilizing slopes and banks, or filling in over rock gardens and retaining walls where a groundcover with more reach than 'Nana' is wanted. Like other forms of the species it is highly drought-tolerant once established and intolerant of soggy, poorly drained soil, so plant it in full sun with sharp drainage. Its vigor and larger scale make it better suited to open groundcover use than to fine bonsai training.
